blocks.title: Head start (Fri to Sun)
blocks.goal: Tools ready, Python bridge done, first concurrent LLM script running before week 1.

tasks.text: Install Python 3.12+ and uv. Create a repo named genai-prep with a README. Put your LLM API key in a .env file and add .env to .gitignore. Make one successful API call from Python. Concrete output: `hello_llm.py` that prints one reply, a README with run steps, and a `.gitignore` that lists `.env`. Interview: you can say you prove a live call works before building anything, and that keys never enter git or logs.
tasks.done_when: A script prints a model reply, and git status shows .env is ignored. Interview angle: walk through key rotation and why you would refuse to log a prompt that might contain PII.

resources.title: uv: Python package and project manager

tasks.text: Type hints, dataclasses and Pydantic models. Read the Pydantic docs overview and models page, then write 3 models including a nested one. Concrete output: `models.py` with three Pydantic models (one nested) and two pytest cases (valid JSON + a readable ValidationError). Interview: you validate LLM JSON at the boundary instead of trusting the model.
tasks.done_when: A nested model validates good JSON and raises a readable error for bad JSON. Interview angle: show the error text you would feed back to the model on a structured-output retry.

tasks.text: Generators, decorators, context managers. Read the two Real Python articles, then write @retry(times=3, backoff=2) and a timing decorator. Concrete output: `retry.py` with `@retry(times=3, backoff=2)`, a timing decorator, and a generator that streams a large file in constant memory, plus tests. Interview: you can name when a decorator beats a wrapper and why generators keep RAG ingest off the heap.
tasks.done_when: A test where a function fails twice then succeeds passes; the generator version of a 1 GB file reader uses constant memory. Interview angle: state time and space of the retry loop and the file reader in one sentence each.

resources.title: How to use generators and yield

tasks.text: async/await in practice. Read the Real Python walkthrough, then call 50 URLs with at most 5 in flight using asyncio.gather and a Semaphore. Concrete output: a script that fetches 50 URLs with `asyncio.Semaphore(5)` and a table of sync vs async wall time. Interview: you can explain why LLM batch jobs need a cap on in-flight calls, not just `gather`.
tasks.done_when: You measured the sync vs async runtime and can explain the difference in one sentence. Interview angle: say what you would do on 429s (backoff + jitter) versus a hung socket (timeout).

resources.title: Async IO in Python: a complete walkthrough

tasks.text: HTTPX streaming and pytest. Stream a response and print chunks as they arrive. Write one pytest test that mocks the HTTP call. Concrete output: a streaming client that prints chunks as they arrive and a pytest that mocks HTTPX so the suite stays offline. Interview: you can explain TTFT versus tokens/sec and why tests must not call a live model.
tasks.done_when: Streaming prints tokens incrementally and the mocked test passes in under a second. Interview angle: describe how you would resume or persist a partial stream if the client disconnects.

tasks.text: Concurrent prompt runner: send 50 prompts with retries, timeout and a rate limit. Print total cost and p50 and p95 latency. Concrete output: a CLI that runs 50 prompts with timeout, retries and a token-bucket, printing cost, p50 and p95. Interview: you treat an LLM call as a fallible RPC with a budget, not a magic function.
tasks.done_when: One command runs 50 prompts; the output shows cost, p50 and p95; a failed call is retried and logged. Interview angle: explain which percentile you would put in an SLO and why a mean latency would hide a bad tail.

tasks.text: Wrap the runner in a FastAPI endpoint with Pydantic request and response models. Concrete output: `POST /run` with Pydantic request/response models and a 422 body you have actually triggered. Interview: you put the schema at the HTTP edge so bad input never reaches the model.
tasks.done_when: POST /run returns validated JSON; invalid input returns a 422 with a clear message. Interview angle: say how you would version this API when the prompt or schema changes.

tasks.text: Push to GitHub with a README. List the three Python features that were new to you. Concrete output: a public or shareable repo whose README lists how to run the runner, the three new Python features, and one measured latency number. Interview: you lead with a number, not a stack list.
tasks.done_when: Repo is public or shareable; README says how to run it. Interview angle: in 30 seconds, pitch this repo as evidence you can ship a concurrent LLM client.

blocks.title: Week 1: Prompting, structured outputs, tool calling
blocks.goal: Ship an extraction API that turns messy documents into validated JSON, with a 50-case eval.

tasks.text: Solve: Two Sum; Contains Duplicate. Pattern: hash map. Concrete output: two solutions with a one-line complexity comment and one extra edge-case test each (empty input; all duplicates). Interview: hash map is the default when you need O(1) membership or complements, at the cost of extra memory.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list, with pattern + complexity said aloud. Interview angle: you can recap Two Sum as 'complement in a map' in 20 seconds.

tasks.text: Prompt anatomy. Read the Anthropic prompt engineering overview (30 min), do the first chapters of the interactive tutorial (45 min), then skim OpenAI's guide for differences (15 min). Concrete output: one file with the same task written five ways and a two-line note on which won and why. Interview: you pick a prompt shape from a measured comparison, not taste.
tasks.done_when: One task written five ways (zero-shot, few-shot, with a role, with XML-style structure, with reasoning) in one file, with a note on which won. Interview angle: say when few-shot beats a longer instruction, and when XML-style tags help a model follow a schema.

tasks.text: Solve: Valid Anagram; Group Anagrams. Pattern: hash map. Concrete output: both solutions plus a test for unicode / mixed case if you have time. Interview: grouping by a canonical key (sorted letters) is the same idea as grouping documents by a fingerprint.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can say why a count-array beats sort when the alphabet is tiny.

tasks.text: Structured outputs. Read the Pydantic and structured-output docs, then try the Instructor library on 10 emails. Concrete output: 10 emails extracted into a Pydantic model, with one forced-invalid case that retries using the validator error. Interview: structured output is a contract; retries are part of the contract, not a hope.
tasks.done_when: Name, date and amount are extracted into a Pydantic model; invalid output triggers one retry that includes the validation error text. Interview angle: name the field that broke most often and how you would change the schema or prompt to fix it.

tasks.text: Solve: Top K Frequent Elements; Product of Array Except Self. Pattern: hash map + heap, prefix/suffix. Concrete output: heap + prefix-suffix solutions with complexity said aloud and one overflow/empty-array edge. Interview: Top-K is the same pattern as 'keep the K most relevant chunks' without sorting the whole list.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can contrast heap Top-K with a full sort in one sentence.

tasks.text: Tool calling end to end. Read the tool-use docs, then build a calculator tool and a lookup tool and run the full loop. Concrete output: a calculator tool and a lookup tool, plus 5 questions that complete the model→tool→result→answer loop and 2 that return a clear tool error. Interview: tool calling is an RPC the model proposes and your code executes under least privilege.
tasks.done_when: Model calls a tool, you execute it, send the result back, and the final answer is correct on 5 test questions; unknown tools and bad arguments return a clear error to the model. Interview angle: walk the sequence on a whiteboard, including what you do when the model invents a tool name.

tasks.text: Solve: Valid Sudoku; Longest Consecutive Sequence. Pattern: hash set. Concrete output: both solutions with a set-based approach and one 'almost valid' Sudoku / duplicate-break edge. Interview: a hash set is the cheap way to ask 'have I seen this?' in a stream.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can state why Longest Consecutive is O(n) only if you start a streak at the minimum.

tasks.text: Context management. Read Anthropic's context engineering post and the prompt caching docs. Skim 'Lost in the Middle'. Use Tiktokenizer to count tokens. Concrete output: a trimmer that keeps a chat under a token budget and a before/after measurement of cache hit latency or cost on a repeated prefix. Interview: context is a scarce resource you allocate, not a dump.
tasks.done_when: A function trims chat history to a token budget; you measured latency or cost with caching on a repeated long prefix. Interview angle: explain lost-in-the-middle and why you would put the question and the best evidence at the edges.

resources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

tasks.text: Implement a token-bucket rate limiter and an exponential backoff with jitter scheduler, with tests. Then solve Valid Palindrome. Concrete output: a token-bucket limiter, backoff-with-jitter, tests that prove burst vs steady rate, and Valid Palindrome. Interview: every production LLM client needs these two primitives before it needs a framework.
tasks.done_when: Limiter allows N calls per second under a burst test; backoff delays grow and are randomized; tests pass. Interview angle: draw the bucket (capacity, refill) and say what a 429 from the provider should do to it.

tasks.text: Eval basics. Read Hamel Husain's two evals posts. Write a 50-case JSONL dataset for your extractor and a scoring script. Concrete output: a 50-row JSONL with inputs and expected fields and a scorer that prints per-field accuracy. Interview: an eval set is the product spec; you do not 'feel' quality.
tasks.done_when: Dataset has inputs and expected fields; the script prints per-field accuracy. Interview angle: name one field you would weight higher than accuracy (e.g. amount or date) and why.

resources.title: LLM Evals: everything you need to know

tasks.text: Extraction API v1: FastAPI POST /extract with a Pydantic schema, retries on invalid output and an async batch endpoint. Concrete output: FastAPI `POST /extract` plus an async batch route, schema validation, and one retry on invalid output. Interview: the API is the product; the model is an implementation detail behind a schema.
tasks.done_when: 10 documents processed in one batch call; invalid outputs retried once; every response validates against the schema. Interview angle: say how you would isolate a single bad document so it does not fail the whole batch.

tasks.text: Collect and label 50 real documents (invoices, emails or resumes with personal data removed) as ground truth. Concrete output: 50 redacted labeled JSON files and a one-line labeling guide in the data README. Interview: ground truth quality bounds every later metric, so you write the rules down.
tasks.done_when: 50 labeled JSON files in a data folder with a README line describing the labeling rules. Interview angle: describe one ambiguous label and the rule you chose so two labelers would agree.

tasks.text: Eval harness: run all 50 documents, report field-level accuracy, p50 and p95 latency and cost per document. Put the first numbers in the README. Concrete output: `make eval` prints field accuracy, p50/p95 and cost per document, and those numbers sit at the top of the README. Interview: you lead a project review with a table, not a demo.
tasks.done_when: make eval prints a table you can paste into the README. Interview angle: pick the one number you would put on a resume line and justify it.

resources.title: A Field Guide to Rapidly Improving AI Products

tasks.text: Prompting, structured output and API questions. Concrete output: spoken answers for each week-1 question, a mark next to hesitations, and one rewritten 4-part outline (what / mechanism / trade-off / measure). Interview: 90 seconds is the real format; notes are a crutch you remove.
tasks.done_when: Answer each question aloud in under 90 seconds without notes. Mark the ones where you hesitated and re-answer them on Wednesday. Interview angle: you can restart a weak answer with 'what / mechanism / trade-off / what I would measure' without looking down.
questions: How do you reduce hallucinations through prompting alone?
Few-shot prompting or fine-tuning: how do you decide?
How do you get reliably valid JSON from a model?
Explain how tool calling works end to end.
What is prompt injection and how would you defend against it?
How do you manage context in a long conversation?
How do you know a prompt change made things better?
How would you call an LLM API 1,000 times safely (concurrency, retries, rate limits, timeouts)?

tasks.text: Redo this week's failed DSA problems. Write five lines on what you learned about prompting. Concrete output: Sunday redo list updated and a five-line prompting note that names one thing that actually moved your extractor score. Interview: you close the week with a number and a mistake, not a topic list.
tasks.done_when: Redo list is empty or scheduled; notes file has five lines; you can state this week's field-accuracy number in one sentence.

blocks.title: Week 2: Transformers, ML basics, first RAG
blocks.goal: Whiteboard the transformer from memory and have a retrieval prototype.

tasks.text: Solve: 3Sum; Container With Most Water. Pattern: two pointers. Concrete output: two-pointer solutions with a 'why not hash/sort' note. Interview: 3Sum and container-with-most-water are the template for shrinking a search space from both ends.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can say when two pointers beat a nested loop without drawing the whole array.

tasks.text: Tokens and embeddings. Watch 3Blue1Brown on transformers (about 30 min), read the Hugging Face tokenizer summary (30 min), then try Tiktokenizer on your own text (15 min). Concrete output: a short note that explains letter-counting failures, number tokenization, and how vocab size hits cost, plus one Tiktokenizer screenshot or count. Interview: tokens are the billing and context unit, not words.
tasks.done_when: You can explain why letter counting and long numbers go wrong for LLMs and how vocabulary size affects cost. Interview angle: give one English sentence and one Hindi/code snippet whose token counts surprised you.

resources.title: Transformers, the tech behind LLMs (Deep Learning Chapter 5)

tasks.text: Solve: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock; Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters. Pattern: sliding window. Concrete output: sliding-window + one-pass stock solutions with edges (empty, strictly decreasing). Interview: a window is how you keep 'the relevant slice' — the same instinct as a context budget.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can state the invariant of the window in one sentence.

problems.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

tasks.text: Attention. Watch 3Blue1Brown on attention (about 30 min), then read The Illustrated Transformer (45 min). Concrete output: a paper diagram of Q, K, V for a 3-token example with every matrix shape labeled. Interview: attention is a weighted sum of values, with weights from scaled query-key scores — not a black box.
tasks.done_when: On paper, compute Q, K, V for a 3-token example and state the shape of every matrix. Interview angle: say why we divide by sqrt(d_k) and what happens to softmax if we do not.

resources.title: Attention in transformers, step-by-step (Deep Learning Chapter 6)

tasks.text: Solve: Longest Repeating Character Replacement; Permutation in String. Pattern: sliding window. Concrete output: both window problems with a frequency-map invariant written above the loop. Interview: you can explain why the window only shrinks, never jumps, on these problems.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: name the map you maintain and the condition that moves `left`.

tasks.text: The transformer block. Explore the Transformer Explainer and LLM Visualization, then watch the part of Umar Jamil's LLaMA lecture on RMSNorm, RoPE and grouped-query attention. Concrete output: a decoder-block sketch from memory with residuals, norms, and shapes, plus a one-liner on RMSNorm, RoPE and GQA. Interview: you can walk a block the way you walk a class diagram.
tasks.done_when: You can draw one decoder block from memory, with residuals and norms in the right place and the shapes labeled. Interview angle: point at residual + norm and say what training problem they fix.

resources.title: LLaMA explained: KV-Cache, RoPE, RMSNorm, GQA, SwiGLU

tasks.text: Solve: Minimum Window Substring. Pattern: sliding window. Take the full hour on this hard problem. Concrete output: a Minimum Window solution (or a honest redo-list entry) with the need-vs-have counts written out. Interview: this is the hard sliding-window; missing the shrink condition is the usual fail.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: solved or on the Sunday redo list, with pattern and complexity said aloud. Interview angle: you can replay one shrink step on a 6-character example.

tasks.text: Decoding and inference. Read The Illustrated GPT-2 and the KV-cache part of the LLaMA lecture. Skim the GQA abstract. Concrete output: the KV-cache memory formula written out and a numeric answer for one real model (layers, kv heads, head dim, bytes, tokens, batch). Interview: prefill is compute-bound; decode is memory-bound because of this cache.
tasks.done_when: You can write the KV-cache memory formula: 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes x tokens x batch, and compute it for one model. Interview angle: compute 7B vs 70B cache at 8K in 16-bit on a whiteboard without a calculator if you can, or show the table.

resources.title: LLaMA explained: KV-Cache, RoPE, RMSNorm, GQA, SwiGLU

tasks.text: Write a byte-pair-encoding trainer: count adjacent pairs on a 1,000-word corpus, merge the most frequent pair 50 times, then encode new text. Then solve Valid Parentheses. Concrete output: a BPE trainer that merges 50 times on 1,000 words, a deterministic second run, and a round-trip encode/decode, plus Valid Parentheses. Interview: BPE is compression of the training text; unseen words still tokenize via subwords.
tasks.done_when: Your merges reproduce on a second run; encode and decode round-trips the text; you can explain the complexity. Interview angle: explain what happens to a brand-new word and why vocab size is a cost knob.

tasks.text: ML basics for interviews. Read the scikit-learn metrics page and watch StatQuest on ROC/AUC and cross-validation. Drill 10 questions. Concrete output: spoken 90-second answers on precision/recall, leakage, overfitting and CV, plus a one-line note on which metric you would pick for a rare failure. Interview: accuracy is a vanity metric on imbalanced labels.
tasks.done_when: You can answer precision vs recall, leakage, overfitting and cross-validation in 90 seconds each. Interview angle: give one leakage example from an LLM eval (test items in the prompt, or future tickets in the train split).

tasks.text: Implement scaled dot-product attention and multi-head attention in PyTorch. Verify against nn.MultiheadAttention. Concrete output: SDPA + MHA in PyTorch that matches `nn.MultiheadAttention` within a tight tolerance, with a causal-mask test. Interview: if you can implement it, you can debug shape errors in anyone's stack.
tasks.done_when: Outputs match to a small tolerance with the same weights; causal mask works. Interview angle: state the Q/K/V shapes for batch B, heads H, seq S, dim D.

resources.title: Let's build GPT: from scratch, in code, spelled out

tasks.text: Implement temperature, top-k and top-p sampling in NumPy and plot the distributions. Concrete output: NumPy samplers for temperature, top-k and top-p plus a plot of the same logits under each filter. Interview: sampling knobs trade diversity against faithfulness; you pick them from the task, not defaults.
tasks.done_when: A plot shows the distribution before and after each filter. Interview angle: say which knob you would freeze for extraction JSON versus a brainstorming assistant.

tasks.text: RAG v0: embed 200 chunks with a sentence-embedding model, store vectors, search by cosine similarity and answer with a citation. Concrete output: 200 embedded chunks, cosine search, and answers that cite a chunk id; 10 hand-picked questions with top-3 recorded. Interview: RAG v0 is retrieve-then-read; you do not skip the citation.
tasks.done_when: A question returns the right chunk in the top 3 on 10 hand-picked questions. Interview angle: name one miss and whether it was chunking, embedding, or the generator.

tasks.text: Tidy RAG v0 into a repo with FAISS or NumPy search, a script to ingest files and a README. Concrete output: a clone-and-run repo (`ingest` + one sample question) that a stranger finishes in under 5 minutes. Interview: a RAG project you cannot rerun is a screenshot, not a system.
tasks.done_when: Fresh clone runs ingest and a sample question in under 5 minutes. Interview angle: write the three commands you would put in the README before any architecture diagram.

tasks.text: Transformer and ML-basics questions. Record yourself explaining the transformer in two minutes. Concrete output: a two-minute transformer recording and spoken answers for the week-2 bank, with hesitations marked. Interview: the two-minute version is what a hiring manager actually hears.
tasks.done_when: Answer each question aloud in under 90 seconds without notes. Mark the ones where you hesitated and re-answer them on Wednesday. Interview angle: restart the transformer answer as tokens → embeddings+positions → attention → FFN → next-token, then one trade-off.
questions: Explain self-attention step by step. Why scale by the square root of d_k?
Why multi-head attention instead of one big head?
Encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder: when would you use each?
Why are positional encodings needed? How does RoPE work at a high level?
What is the KV cache, why does it speed up generation, and what does it cost?
Why is attention O(n^2) and how do FlashAttention and grouped-query attention help?
How does BPE work? What happens to words the vocabulary has never seen?
What do temperature, top-k and top-p each do?
Precision vs recall: give a case where each matters more. Why is accuracy misleading on imbalanced data?
What is data leakage? Give three examples and how you would prevent each.

tasks.text: Redo failed DSA problems. Add attention, KV cache and sampling notes to your notes file. Concrete output: redo list updated and a notes section on attention, KV cache and sampling with one formula and one plot reference. Interview: you can retrieve those notes as a 60-second recap.
tasks.done_when: Redo list is empty or scheduled; notes file has attention, KV cache and sampling; you can state the KV-cache formula without opening it.

blocks.title: Week 3: RAG end to end
blocks.goal: A RAG app on a real corpus with a 100-question golden set and measured improvements.

tasks.text: Solve: Daily Temperatures; Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation. Pattern: monotonic stack, stack. Concrete output: monotonic-stack and RPN solutions with one 'why a stack' sentence each. Interview: Daily Temperatures is the template for 'next greater'; RPN is the template for evaluating a plan.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can draw the stack after three temperatures.

tasks.text: Ingestion and chunking. Read Chroma's chunking evaluation and skim Anthropic's contextual retrieval post. Look at Unstructured for parsing PDFs. Concrete output: a table of three chunkers (fixed, recursive, heading-aware) on 20 questions with a winner and a loser. Interview: chunk size is a measured hyperparameter, not 512 because a blog said so.
tasks.done_when: Three chunkers compared on 20 questions in one table: fixed-size, recursive and heading-aware. Interview angle: say which question type heading-aware won on, and which it lost.

tasks.text: Solve: Largest Rectangle in Histogram; Binary Search. Pattern: binary search, monotonic stack. Concrete output: histogram + binary-search solutions; write the search invariant in a comment. Interview: binary search on an answer space (capacity, speed) shows up in batching and rate math.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: state the monotonic predicate you binary-search on.

tasks.text: Embeddings and vector stores. Read Pinecone's HNSW explainer, skim the pgvector README and Qdrant filtering docs, and look at the MTEB leaderboard. Concrete output: a short note on HNSW parameters (M, efConstruction, efSearch) and a recall-vs-latency sentence, plus why you might still pick pgvector. Interview: ANN is an approximation you pay for with recall.
tasks.done_when: You can explain M, efConstruction and efSearch and the recall versus latency tradeoff. Interview angle: pick one parameter you would raise to buy recall and name the cost.

tasks.text: Solve: Koko Eating Bananas; Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array. Pattern: binary search, binary search on answer. Concrete output: Koko + rotated-min solutions with the binary-search-on-answer predicate written out. Interview: you search the answer, not the index, when the predicate is monotonic.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: say why Koko's `hours(speed)` is monotonic.

problems.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

tasks.text: Hybrid search. Read Weaviate's hybrid search article and the contextual retrieval results. Implement BM25 plus vector search with Reciprocal Rank Fusion. Concrete output: BM25 + vector + RRF on 20 questions and a recall@5 before/after. Interview: hybrid exists because embeddings miss identifiers and BM25 misses paraphrases.
tasks.done_when: Hybrid recall@5 on 20 questions is higher or you can explain why it is not. Interview angle: give one query hybrid saved and one it did not, and what you would try next (rerank, rewrite).

tasks.text: Solve: Search in Rotated Sorted Array; Time Based Key-Value Store. Pattern: binary search, binary search + hash map. Concrete output: rotated-search + time-based KV solutions; mention how the KV store is a tiny version of a feature store. Interview: binary search plus a map is how you query 'as of time t'.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can explain the two-array / two-map layout of the time store in 30 seconds.

tasks.text: Reranking and query transformation. Add a cross-encoder reranker to the top 30 results and try HyDE on 10 hard questions. Concrete output: a cross-encoder over the top 30, a top-5 cut, HyDE on 10 hard questions, and the added milliseconds written down. Interview: rerank spends compute on a shortlist; HyDE spends a generation to improve the query.
tasks.done_when: A reranker takes the top 30 to the top 5; you recorded the added latency. Interview angle: say when HyDE hurts (precise identifiers) and when a reranker is not worth the p95 hit.

resources.title: Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE)

tasks.text: Write a sliding-window chunker with overlap and a Reciprocal Rank Fusion function, both with tests. Concrete output: a sliding-window chunker with overlap tests (no dropped text) and an RRF function checked against a hand-worked example. Interview: these two functions are the unglamorous core of a RAG repo.
tasks.done_when: Chunker never drops text and respects the overlap; RRF merges two ranked lists correctly on a hand-worked example. Interview angle: write the RRF formula (`1/(k+rank)`) and pick a k, with a reason.

tasks.text: RAG evaluation. Read the Ragas docs and the Seven Failure Points paper. Write the golden-set spec: 100 questions with source passage ids, 20 of them unanswerable. Concrete output: a golden-set spec for 100 questions (20 unanswerable) with source passage ids and an answerable flag. Interview: you evaluate retrieval and generation separately or you cannot debug.
tasks.done_when: Spec lists question, expected answer, source passage ids and whether answerable. Interview angle: name the metric you would look at first when answers are wrong (recall@k, not the judge).

resources.title: Seven Failure Points When Engineering a RAG System
LLM Evals: everything you need to know

tasks.text: Pick a public corpus (documentation of a tool you use, a set of papers, or public FAQs) and write the 100-question golden set. Concrete output: 100 questions on a real public corpus, 20 unanswerable, each with source ids you can open. Interview: the golden set is the hardest part of the project and the part most candidates skip.
tasks.done_when: 100 questions, 20 unanswerable, each with source ids. Interview angle: describe how you sampled questions so you did not only test headings the chunker already loves.

tasks.text: Pipeline v1: parse, chunk, embed, store, retrieve, answer with citations; abstain when the context lacks the answer. Concrete output: parse→chunk→embed→store→retrieve→answer with citations, and a refusal when context cannot support the claim. Interview: abstention is a feature; a fluent guess is a bug.
tasks.done_when: Answers include citations that map to source URLs; unanswerable questions get a refusal, not a guess. Interview angle: show one refusal and the rule that triggered it (no supporting chunk, or citation verifier fail).

tasks.text: Add BM25 hybrid search and a reranker. Record recall@5, MRR, faithfulness and latency before and after each change. Concrete output: a README table with one row per change (hybrid, rerank) listing recall@5, MRR, faithfulness and latency, plus a one-line conclusion each. Interview: you ship ablations, not vibes.
tasks.done_when: A table in the README with one row per change and a one-line conclusion for each. Interview angle: name the change you would revert because the latency cost was not worth the recall.

tasks.text: RAG questions. Concrete output: spoken answers for the RAG bank and one 4-part outline for 'debug a wrong RAG answer'. Interview: the debug walk (retrieve vs rank vs generate) is the question they will actually ask.
tasks.done_when: Answer each question aloud in under 90 seconds without notes. Mark the ones where you hesitated and re-answer them on Wednesday. Interview angle: you can start with 'I log one failing query end to end' without a pause.
questions: Design a RAG system for 1 million documents. Walk through every component.
How do you choose chunk size and overlap, and how would you test it?
Dense vs sparse vs hybrid retrieval: what does a reranker add?
How do you evaluate retrieval separately from generation?
Explain HNSW at a high level and its tradeoffs.
How do you make sure users only retrieve documents they may access?
How do you keep an index fresh as documents change?
Your RAG answers are wrong. Walk me through debugging it.

tasks.text: Redo failed DSA problems. Write down the 5 worst RAG failures from your eval and the cause of each. Concrete output: redo list updated and five RAG failures tagged with stage (chunk / retrieve / rank / generate) and a next fix. Interview: a failure taxonomy is more impressive than a demo.
tasks.done_when: Redo list is empty or scheduled; five failures have a cause and a next experiment; you can recite the worst one.

blocks.title: Week 4: Agents, tools, MCP
blocks.goal: An agent with tools, limits and tracing, a small MCP server and a 20-task eval.

tasks.text: Solve: Reverse Linked List; Merge Two Sorted Lists. Pattern: linked list. Concrete output: reverse and merge-list solutions with pointer diagrams in a comment if you needed them. Interview: list reversal is the interview's way of asking whether you can mutate pointers without losing the rest of the list.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can reverse a 3-node list aloud, naming `prev`, `cur`, `next`.

tasks.text: Workflows vs agents. Read Anthropic's Building Effective Agents, Cognition's counterpoint and OpenAI's guide. Concrete output: a one-page workflow-vs-agent table with three real examples and a default of 'workflow unless the path is unknown'. Interview: an agent is a loop you cannot fully specify; most products should not start there.
tasks.done_when: A one-page table of when to use a workflow versus an agent, with three examples. Interview angle: give one task you would refuse to agent-ify and the cheaper chain you would ship instead.

resources.title: A practical guide to building agents

tasks.text: Solve: Linked List Cycle; Remove Nth Node From End of List. Pattern: fast and slow pointers, linked list. Concrete output: cycle detect + remove-nth solutions using two pointers. Interview: fast/slow is how you find a cycle or the k-th from the end without a length pass.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can say why the gap of n between pointers finds the node to delete.

problems.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List

tasks.text: The agent loop and tool design. Read Lilian Weng's agents post, the ReAct paper abstract and Anthropic's post on writing tools. Concrete output: a rewritten tool description after you watched the model misuse the first one, plus a short ReAct failure-mode list. Interview: tool quality is prompt engineering for actions; vague tools get abused.
tasks.done_when: You rewrote the description of one tool after seeing the model misuse it. Interview angle: show the before/after description and the misuse it stopped.

tasks.text: Solve: Invert Binary Tree; Maximum Depth of Binary Tree. Pattern: tree DFS. Concrete output: invert + max-depth solutions written as both recursive and (if you have time) iterative. Interview: tree DFS is the shape of walking a plan or a file tree.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: state the base case and the combine step in one line each.

tasks.text: Memory, planning and context for long runs. Read Anthropic's context engineering post and Chip Huyen's Agents post. Concrete output: a diagram of working context, a long-term store, and the trigger that summarizes or offloads. Interview: memory is a product decision (what to persist, when to forget), not a vector DB logo.
tasks.done_when: A diagram of short-term context, a long-term store and a summarization trigger. Interview angle: say what you would never put in long-term memory (secrets, stale ACLs) and how a user deletes it.

resources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

tasks.text: Solve: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal; Validate Binary Search Tree. Pattern: BST, tree BFS. Concrete output: level-order and BST-validate solutions; mention BFS vs inorder. Interview: level-order is the template for 'process a frontier'; BST validate is 'bounds travel with the recursion'.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can state the low/high bounds you pass down on validate.

tasks.text: MCP. Read the MCP introduction, run a sample server from the Python SDK and call it from a client. Concrete output: a sample MCP server running locally and a client that lists then calls one tool. Interview: MCP is a standard for exposing tools; it does not make those tools safe.
tasks.done_when: A sample MCP server runs and a client lists and calls its tools. Interview angle: name one thing you would still wrap (auth, allow-list, timeouts) even if the client 'just speaks MCP'.

tasks.text: Implement an LRU cache with O(1) get and put, and add a TTL. Then solve Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST. Concrete output: LRU+TTL with eviction and expiry tests, plus BST LCA. Interview: LRU is hashmap + doubly linked list; this is also how you would expire agent scratchpads.
tasks.done_when: Cache passes eviction and expiry tests; you can explain why a doubly linked list plus a hash map gives O(1). Interview angle: explain O(1) move-to-front and what a TTL expiry does to the list and the map.

problems.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST

tasks.text: Agent reliability. Read Anthropic's multi-agent research system post and set up Langfuse tracing. Read Simon Willison on the lethal trifecta. Concrete output: eight agent failure modes each with a mitigation, and one Langfuse (or similar) trace you can open. Interview: reliability is limits + traces + least privilege, not a smarter loop.
tasks.done_when: A list of 8 failure modes with a mitigation each; one run is visible in a trace. Interview angle: pick the lethal-trifecta risk that scares you most on your own agent and the control you added.

resources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system
The lethal trifecta for AI agents

tasks.text: Agent loop in plain Python (under 150 lines) with 3 tools, a step limit, a cost limit and full trace logging. Concrete output: <150-line Python loop, 3 tools, step and cost caps, and a JSONL trace of every step. Interview: if you cannot write the loop, you cannot debug a framework's loop.
tasks.done_when: Agent solves 5 sample tasks; it stops at the step limit; every step is in the trace. Interview angle: show the stop condition that fired on a runaway task and the trace line that proved it.

tasks.text: Write a 20-task eval suite for the agent with a pass condition for each task. Concrete output: 20 tasks with an explicit pass condition and a script that prints success rate, average steps and cost. Interview: agent evals score trajectories, not just final strings.
tasks.done_when: A script runs all 20 tasks and prints success rate, average steps and cost. Interview angle: name a task that passed the final answer but should have failed on a bad tool call, and how you scored it.

tasks.text: Build an MCP server with 2 tools of your own and call it from your agent. Concrete output: an MCP server with two of your tools wired into the agent, plus a clear error when a tool fails. Interview: you can put a real system behind MCP without giving the model a shell.
tasks.done_when: Agent uses an MCP tool to finish a task; tool errors return clear messages. Interview angle: walk one successful MCP call and one tool error from the trace.

tasks.text: Agent questions. Concrete output: spoken answers for the agent bank and a 4-part outline for 'workflow vs agent'. Interview: they will ask when you would not use an agent; have a crisp no.
tasks.done_when: Answer each question aloud in under 90 seconds without notes. Mark the ones where you hesitated and re-answer them on Wednesday. Interview angle: you can name two failure modes of ReAct and the cap you use for each (steps, cost, approvals).
questions: What is the difference between a workflow and an agent? When would you avoid an agent?
Explain the ReAct loop and its failure modes.
How do you make an agent reliable and keep its cost bounded?
How would you design memory for a long-running assistant?
What is MCP and what problem does it solve?
Single agent vs multi-agent: what are the tradeoffs?
How do you evaluate an agent and debug a bad trajectory?
How do you stop an agent from taking a harmful action?

tasks.text: Record success rate, average steps and cost in the README. Redo failed DSA problems. Concrete output: README numbers (success rate, steps, cost) and a clean Sunday redo list. Interview: an agent project without those three numbers is unfinished.
tasks.done_when: README has the three numbers; redo list is empty or scheduled; you can quote the success rate without opening the file.

blocks.title: Week 5: LLM internals, serving, production, security
blocks.goal: Deploy a service with CI evals and tracing, and run one LoRA fine-tune.

tasks.text: Solve: Kth Largest Element in a Stream; K Closest Points to Origin. Pattern: heap. Concrete output: heap solutions for stream kth-largest and k-closest, with a note on why a heap beats a full sort in a stream. Interview: online Top-K is how you would keep 'interesting traces' without storing all of them.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: state heap size and the invariant after each insert.

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream

tasks.text: The LLM lifecycle. Watch Karpathy's Deep Dive into LLMs, first half (pretraining and post-training), and skim the InstructGPT abstract. Concrete output: a 2-minute spoken narration of pretraining → SFT → preference training (RLHF/DPO) and what each stage changes. Interview: pretraining is knowledge and fluency; post-training is behavior.
tasks.done_when: You can narrate pretraining, SFT and RLHF in 2 minutes and say what each stage changes. Interview angle: say one thing fine-tuning will not add (fresh private facts) and what you would use instead (RAG).

resources.title: Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT
Training language models to follow instructions (InstructGPT)

tasks.text: Solve: Number of Islands; Clone Graph. Pattern: graph + hash map, graph DFS/BFS. Concrete output: islands + clone-graph with a visited set; mention why clone needs the map. Interview: graphs plus a hash map is how you walk a tool-dependency or citation graph without looping.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can clone a 3-node cycle aloud.

tasks.text: Quantization and memory math. Read the visual guide to quantization and Kipply's inference arithmetic. Compute weights and KV cache for a 7B and a 70B model. Concrete output: a table of 7B and 70B weight memory at 16/8/4-bit plus KV cache at 8K. Interview: you do the arithmetic before you pick a GPU or a quantized API.
tasks.done_when: A table of memory for 7B and 70B at 16-bit, 8-bit and 4-bit, plus KV cache at 8K context. Interview angle: point at the row where the cache, not the weights, becomes the limiter.

tasks.text: Solve: Course Schedule; Course Schedule II. Pattern: topological sort. Concrete output: both course-schedule solutions (cycle detect + order). Interview: topo sort is how you order agent tools or DAG workflows and how you refuse a cycle.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can say what a cycle means in a 'tool A needs tool B' graph.

tasks.text: Serving. Read the vLLM PagedAttention post, Hugging Face's continuous batching article and the BentoML inference handbook. Concrete output: a one-page note on prefill vs decode, continuous batching and PagedAttention you can recite. Interview: serving is a scheduler problem; the model is the payload.
tasks.done_when: You can explain prefill vs decode, continuous batching and PagedAttention without notes. Interview angle: explain which phase you are in for a 4k-token prompt with a 20-token answer, and which optimization helps which phase.

resources.title: vLLM: easy, fast and cheap LLM serving with PagedAttention

tasks.text: Solve: Merge Intervals; Insert Interval. Pattern: intervals. Concrete output: merge + insert interval solutions sorted by start. Interview: intervals are calendar math and also 'merge overlapping retrieval windows'.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can merge three overlapping ranges aloud.

tasks.text: Cost, routing and observability. Read Eugene Yan's patterns post and the prompt caching docs. Sketch a routing rule: cheap model first, escalate on low confidence. Concrete output: a routing/caching plan with expected savings and the quality risk of each rule (cheap first, escalate on low confidence, cache the prefix). Interview: cost is a product feature you design, not a bill you regret.
tasks.done_when: A written routing and caching plan with expected savings and the quality risk. Interview angle: pick the one cache key you would use and what invalidates it.

resources.title: Patterns for Building LLM-based Systems and Products

tasks.text: Implement cosine-similarity top-k search over 100,000 random vectors using NumPy, then using a heap. Write a topological sort that orders agent tools by dependency. Concrete output: NumPy and heap top-k over 100k vectors with matching results and timings, plus a topo sort that detects a cycle in tool deps. Interview: you can implement the primitives your vector DB and agent DAG sit on.
tasks.done_when: Both versions return the same top 10; you timed them; the topological sort detects a cycle. Interview angle: say which version you would ship at 100k vs 10M vectors and why.

resources.title: Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using HNSW

tasks.text: Security. Read the OWASP LLM Top 10 and Simon Willison's prompt-injection series. Play Gandalf for 30 minutes. Concrete output: one indirect-injection story and five layered defenses, plus 30 minutes of Gandalf notes. Interview: assume the model can be fooled; design so the blast radius is small.
tasks.done_when: You can give an indirect injection example and 5 layered defenses. Interview angle: order your five defenses from 'stops the action' to 'detects after the fact'.

resources.title: Not what you've signed up for: indirect prompt injection

tasks.text: Dockerize your RAG or extraction service. Add API-key auth and rate limiting. Concrete output: a Dockerfile that boots the RAG or extraction service with API-key auth and a rate limit. Interview: if it is not runnable by someone else, it is not a service.
tasks.done_when: docker run starts the service; unauthenticated requests are rejected. Interview angle: say where the key lives (env, not image) and what an unauthenticated request returns.

tasks.text: GitHub Actions pipeline: lint, tests, then your eval suite with a score threshold; deploy to a cloud service. Concrete output: a GitHub Actions workflow (lint, tests, eval threshold) that fails a PR you deliberately worsen. Interview: eval-in-CI is how you keep a prompt change from shipping a silent regression.
tasks.done_when: A pull request that lowers the eval score fails the build. Interview angle: show the failing check and the threshold you chose, and why it is not 100%.

tasks.text: Add tracing and a dashboard for latency, tokens and cost. Concrete output: traces plus a dashboard where you can sort by latency and cost and open the worst request. Interview: observability is how you debug production; logs of full prompts are a privacy bug.
tasks.done_when: You can find your slowest and most expensive request from the dashboard. Interview angle: name the slowest request you found and whether it was prefill, retrieval, or the reranker.

tasks.text: LoRA fine-tune of a small open model on 1,000 to 2,000 examples in Colab. Compare with the base model on a held-out set. Concrete output: a LoRA run on 1–2k examples and a table of base vs prompted vs fine-tuned on ≥50 held-out rows. Interview: fine-tune to change behavior or cost, not to add facts you could retrieve.
tasks.done_when: A table of base vs prompted vs fine-tuned on at least 50 held-out examples. Interview angle: say whether LoRA earned its place on that table, and what you would do if it overfit.

resources.title: LoRA explained visually plus PyTorch code from scratch

tasks.text: Red-team your app with 10 injection and data-leak attempts. Record what worked. Concrete output: 10 injection/leak attempts with result and one shipped fix. Interview: red-teaming is an eval set; a one-off chat with the app does not count.
tasks.done_when: A short list of attacks, results and one fix. Interview angle: describe the attack that worked and the control that stopped a replay.

tasks.text: LLM, serving and security questions. Concrete output: spoken answers for the LLM/serving/security bank and one 4-part outline for 'cut cost 50%'. Interview: they want a menu (cache, route, shrink context, distill) with what you would measure after each.
tasks.done_when: Answer each question aloud in under 90 seconds without notes. Mark the ones where you hesitated and re-answer them on Wednesday. Interview angle: you can start the cost answer with a baseline spend and three cuts that do not touch the golden-set score.
questions: Walk through the LLM training pipeline from pretraining to deployment.
RAG vs fine-tuning: when do you pick each, and when both?
Explain LoRA. Why is it parameter-efficient? What is QLoRA?
RLHF vs DPO: what does each do and why did DPO become popular?
How much GPU memory do you need to serve a 70B model in 16-bit vs 4-bit, before the KV cache?
Explain prefill vs decode and which one limits you in each case.
What is continuous batching? What is PagedAttention?
Give an example of indirect prompt injection and your layered defenses.
How would you cut the cost of an LLM feature by 50% without hurting quality?

tasks.text: Update READMEs with numbers. Redo failed DSA problems. Concrete output: READMEs updated with this week's numbers and a clean redo list. Interview: every project you will talk about has a metric on the first screen.
tasks.done_when: READMEs show current numbers; redo list is empty or scheduled; you can quote one serving or security number.

blocks.title: Week 6: System design, mocks, applications
blocks.goal: Rehearse the interview loop end to end and start applying.

tasks.text: Solve: Climbing Stairs; Coin Change. Pattern: dynamic programming. First look at dynamic programming: define the state, then the recurrence. Concrete output: climbing-stairs + coin-change with state and recurrence written before code. Interview: DP is 'define the subproblem'; coin-change is also how you talk about minimum tool calls to reach a goal.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can say the recurrence for coin-change without opening the file.

tasks.text: System design framework and Design 1: support chatbot over 50,000 help articles. Read Chip Huyen's platform post first (30 min). Then 45 minutes timed on paper, 15 minutes to compare. Concrete output: a one-page design for a 50k-article support bot (questions, metrics, estimates, architecture, two deep dives, eval, rollout) after a 45-minute timed pass. Interview: you start from SLOs and corpus, not from a framework.
tasks.done_when: One page with clarifying questions, metrics, estimates, architecture, two deep dives, evaluation and rollout. Interview angle: name the first two clarifying questions you asked and the metric you would put on the launch dashboard.

resources.title: Genie: Uber's Gen AI on-call copilot

tasks.text: Solve: Edit Distance; Longest Common Subsequence. Pattern: dynamic programming. Used in evaluation metrics such as WER and ROUGE-L. Concrete output: edit-distance + LCS with the DP table story; note WER and ROUGE-L. Interview: these are the metrics hiding inside 'the summary looks good'.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can say what a high edit distance means for an ASR or agent transcript.

tasks.text: Design 2: enterprise search with per-user permissions. Read Slack's secure-AI post. Timed 45 minutes, then compare. Concrete output: a 45-minute enterprise-search design that filters by permission before retrieval and says how ACL revokes propagate. Interview: post-filter is a leak; ACLs are index data.
tasks.done_when: Your design filters by permission before retrieval and says how ACL changes propagate. Interview angle: walk a revoke: what you update, how soon a forbidden chunk disappears, and the test that proves it.

resources.title: How we built Slack AI to be secure and private

tasks.text: Solve: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree); Find Median from Data Stream. Pattern: trie, two heaps. Timed mock: 2 problems in 45 minutes, talking aloud. Concrete output: a 45-minute timed pair (trie + two-heap median) talking aloud. Interview: a trie is prefix search; two heaps keep a running median — both show up in autocomplete and streaming analytics.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you said complexity before coding, on the recording if you made one.

tasks.text: Design 3: coding assistant in an IDE. Read GitHub's post on the LLMs behind Copilot. Timed 45 minutes, then compare. Concrete output: a 45-minute IDE-assistant design with a latency budget and a clear story of what you retrieve from the repo (symbols, not whole files). Interview: the product is retrieve-the-right-code plus a cheap verify (tests).
tasks.done_when: Design states a latency budget and what context is retrieved from the repo. Interview angle: give the p95 you promised and which context you would drop first to hit it.

resources.title: Inside GitHub: working with the LLMs behind GitHub Copilot

tasks.text: Solve: Word Break; Subsets. Pattern: backtracking, dynamic programming. Timed mock: 2 problems in 45 minutes, talking aloud. Concrete output: a 45-minute timed pair (word-break + subsets) talking aloud. Interview: word-break is DP + dictionary; subsets is backtracking — say the pattern before you type.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can state the word-break recurrence and the subset choose/skip.

tasks.text: Design 4: autonomous research agent. Reread Anthropic's multi-agent research post. Timed 45 minutes, then compare. Concrete output: a 45-minute research-agent design with cost caps, citation checks and a trajectory eval. Interview: multi-agent is a cost and coordination choice you can defend with a number, not a default.
tasks.done_when: Design includes cost caps, citation checks and how you evaluate trajectories. Interview angle: say how you would kill a runaway worker and how a citation-less claim is scored.

resources.title: How we built our multi-agent research system

tasks.text: Solve: Rotting Oranges; Merge k Sorted Lists. Pattern: heap, multi-source BFS. Timed mock: 2 problems in 45 minutes, talking aloud. Concrete output: a 45-minute timed pair (rotting oranges + merge-k lists). Interview: multi-source BFS and a heap of k heads are the two 'process many frontiers' templates.
tasks.done_when: For each problem you named the pattern, stated time and space complexity aloud and tested one edge case. Anything you could not finish in 30 minutes goes on the redo list for Sunday. Concrete output: both problems solved or on the Sunday redo list. Interview angle: you can say why rotting oranges is BFS on time, not DFS.

tasks.text: Design 5: text-to-SQL analyst (or a voice agent). Read Pinterest's text-to-SQL post. Then write your 6 STAR stories. Concrete output: a text-to-SQL (or voice) design plus six STAR stories, each with a number in the Result. Interview: stories without a number are opinions; designs without guardrails are demos.
tasks.done_when: Six STAR stories each with a number in the Result. Interview angle: recite one STAR in 60 seconds and point at the number in the Result.

resources.title: How we built Text-to-SQL at Pinterest
Musings on building a generative AI product

tasks.text: Two timed coding mocks (45 minutes each), recorded. Review the recordings for unclear structure and missing complexity statements. Concrete output: two recorded 45-minute coding mocks and a review note on structure and missing complexity. Interview: the recording is how you find that you never said Big-O.
tasks.done_when: Answer each question aloud in under 90 seconds without notes. Mark the ones where you hesitated and re-answer them on Wednesday. Interview angle: you can name the one habit you will change in the next mock (e.g. restate, then complexity, then code).
questions: Pick the two weakest DSA patterns from your redo list and solve a fresh medium from each.

tasks.text: One full system design mock, recorded, then a 30-minute fundamentals Q&A on transformers, RAG and agents. Concrete output: one recorded system-design mock and a 30-minute fundamentals Q&A covering transformers, RAG and agents. Interview: they will bounce between design and fundamentals in the same hour.
tasks.done_when: Answer each question aloud in under 90 seconds without notes. Mark the ones where you hesitated and re-answer them on Wednesday. Interview angle: you have a 90-second transformer, a RAG debug walk, and a 'when not to agent' answer ready.
questions: Design a RAG assistant for 1 million documents with permission-aware search.
How would you reduce latency from 6 seconds to under 2 seconds?

tasks.text: Polish your three best projects: README opens with the problem and headline metric, architecture diagram, results table, failure analysis, live link or recording. Concrete output: three project READMEs that open with problem + headline metric, plus diagram, results table, failures, and a live link or recording. Interview: a reviewer should understand each repo in 3 minutes without you on the call.
tasks.done_when: A reviewer can understand each project in 3 minutes. Interview angle: pick the metric on each README and the failure you will volunteer before they ask.

tasks.text: Resume to one page with a measured result on every project. Update LinkedIn and GitHub profile. Concrete output: a one-page resume where every project line has a number, plus LinkedIn/GitHub that match. Interview: if the number is not on the resume, it will not come up.
tasks.done_when: Each project line has a number. Interview angle: you can defend each number (what you measured, on what set) if a recruiter asks 'is this real?'.

resources.title: Introduction to Machine Learning Interviews Book

tasks.text: List 30 target companies and roles. Apply to the first 10. Concrete output: a 30-row target list and 10 applications sent, with date and referral column. Interview: volume without a fit story is spam; you can say why each of the 10.
tasks.done_when: A spreadsheet with company, role, date applied and referral contact. Interview angle: name the role you are strongest for and the project you would lead with.

tasks.text: Full question bank round: answer 25 questions aloud across all modules and mark the weak ones. Concrete output: 25 spoken answers across the bank and a short weak-list for next week's mocks. Interview: coverage beats polishing the five questions you like.
tasks.done_when: Answer each question aloud in under 90 seconds without notes. Mark the ones where you hesitated and re-answer them on Wednesday. Interview angle: you know the three questions you still owe a 4-part answer, and you will drill them first tomorrow.
questions: Use the question lists from weeks 1 to 5; pick 5 from each.

tasks.text: Final review: tick the readiness checklist in the course doc and plan the next two weeks of mocks and applications. Concrete output: the course readiness checklist ticked and a two-week calendar of mocks and applications. Interview: the sprint ends with a plan, not a feeling that you are 'ready'.
tasks.done_when: Readiness checklist ticked; next two weeks have dated mocks and application targets; you can say the first next action.
